title: The Dean of Santiago and Don Illan
text:
In a tale told by the Spanish prince Don Juan Manuel, the dean of Santiago came to Toledo to learn magic from the famous master Don Illan. Don Illan was reluctant. Men who rose to high places, he said, soon forgot those who had helped them. The dean swore he would never forget, and he would grant Don Illan whatever he asked. Don Illan quietly told his housekeeper to get partridges ready for dinner but not to cook them until he gave the order.

Then messengers arrived. The dean's uncle, the archbishop of Santiago, was ill, then dead, and the dean was elected in his place. Don Illan asked that his son receive the vacant deanship. The new archbishop gave it to his own brother instead, promising something better later. Soon he was made bishop of Toulouse, then cardinal, then pope. Each time Don Illan asked for something for his son, and each time the post went to a relative or friend, with fresh promises.

At last, as pope, he told Don Illan to stop asking or he would throw him in prison as a heretic and sorcerer. Don Illan replied that since there was nothing for him, he would just have to eat the partridges he had ordered for dinner.

At that moment the dean found himself back in Toledo, still a dean, in Don Illan's house. Everything had been an illusion. Don Illan sent him home ashamed, without even sharing the partridges.
lesson: Notice how people treat you when they no longer need you, ideally before you have given them everything. And keep your own promises once you rise.
people: Don Illan of Toledo, the dean of Santiago
source: Don Juan Manuel, El Conde Lucanor, Exemplo 11
